ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest filings and earnings-call evidence on net revenue retention, gross payment volume, location growth, attach rates for payroll/loyalty/marketing, churn by restaurant segment, and whether operator cost pressure is slowing software adoption.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Toast is the cleanest public-market mapping to the restaurant technology chokepoint: POS, payments, digital ordering, loyalty, menu control, labor tools, and operator data workflows. If restaurants remain pressured by labor, food costs, and value-seeking consumers, the operating-system layer can become a durable productivity node rather than just discretionary software spend.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need most recent company-level data separating traffic, price, mix, promotional impact, loyalty contribution, franchisee cash flow, and international market performance.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: McDonald's is the global benchmark for the consumer value, traffic, digital loyalty, beverage, breakfast, and franchisee-unit-economics node. It is prioritized because it can validate or falsify whether large QSR systems can defend traffic with value menus and loyalty without materially impairing franchisee margins.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest volume trends, independent-restaurant case growth, gross margin by category, private-label penetration, inflation/deflation pass-through, and customer retention data.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Sysco is the largest broadline foodservice distribution node in the chunk and maps directly to restaurant replenishment, food-cost management, private-label substitution, and independent-restaurant health. It is a high-value upstream read-through for whether operators are consolidating purchasing and seeking distributor-led menu-cost support.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current revenue mix, ARR growth, customer wins/losses, enterprise QSR penetration, margin trajectory, acquisition integration evidence, and proof that products are mission-critical rather than replaceable modules.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: PAR is a focused restaurant-tech supplier tied to QSR infrastructure, loyalty, ordering, payments, and operational optimization. Its public-market purity and potential bottleneck exposure are strong, but evidence quality and risk clarity are lower than larger peers because more work is needed on customer concentration, integration progress, profitability, and competitive position.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest restaurant-specific order growth, take-rate trends, ad revenue contribution, DashPass engagement, merchant churn, regulatory labor-cost exposure, and separation of restaurant delivery from grocery and broader local commerce.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: DoorDash is a high-signal off-premises restaurant demand and logistics-density node. It can show whether consumers continue to pay for convenience, whether subscription engagement supports frequency, and whether merchants tolerate delivery economics under margin pressure.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need brand-level traffic, franchisee economics, Taco Bell versus KFC/Pizza Hut divergence, loyalty engagement, international unit economics, and promotional margin impact.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Yum is a strong multi-brand QSR franchisor read-through, especially through Taco Bell's value, menu innovation, digital, loyalty, and beverage/daypart potential. It ranks below McDonald's because brand-mix complexity makes the signal less pure, but it remains a key global franchise-system test case.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest traffic versus check split, beef-cost outlook, labor-cost trend, store-level margin, wait-time/throughput evidence, and whether value perception is sustainable as menu prices rise.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Texas Roadhouse is a high-signal casual-dining operator because it tests whether traffic-positive comps and perceived value can persist despite beef-cost pressure. It is less of a supply-chain chokepoint than Toast, Sysco, or PAR, but it has excellent public-market purity and falsifiability.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current traffic versus pricing, transaction throughput, digital order mix, labor productivity, protein/input inflation sensitivity, and proof that premium fast casual can sustain margins without excessive price reliance.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Chipotle is a high-quality fast-casual throughput and digital-ordering benchmark. Its evidence quality and public-market purity are strong, but Serenity priority is moderated because the market usually recognizes the quality, reducing mispricing potential versus less obvious chokepoint nodes.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest filings/earnings evidence for independent restaurant case growth, exclusive-brand mix, gross-margin bridge, customer retention, and whether menu-engineering tools are driving measurable share gains rather than normal distribution volume.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Best Serenity-style chokepoint candidate in this chunk because it sits between restaurant operators and food/input cost pressure. If restaurants face persistent labor, commodity, and menu-pricing constraints, a broadline distributor with scale, private/exclusive brands, purchasing data, menu tools, and operator services may be a cleaner way to study cost-control demand than any single restaurant brand. Public-market purity is high because foodservice distribution is the core business, and the thesis is highly falsifiable through case volume, independent restaurant demand, gross margin, private-label penetration, and operator retention.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need recent restaurant customer volume, private-label mix, segment margin, debt/leverage sensitivity, inflation pass-through, and relative share gains versus Sysco, US Foods, and specialty distributors.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Performance Food Group is a strong secondary foodservice distribution candidate, exposed to restaurant sourcing, private-label inputs, and purchasing consolidation. It is slightly lower than Sysco because the broadline-distribution scarcity signal is less dominant and requires more company-specific validation.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need updated same-restaurant sales split between traffic and price, new-unit productivity, cannibalization, margin by cohort, digital mix, labor efficiency, and evidence that growth is not dependent on temporary novelty.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: CAVA is a pure fast-casual growth concept and a useful test of whether health, customization, digital ordering, throughput, and perceived food quality can support traffic while the unit base expands. It is prioritized for demand durability and falsifiability, though its chokepoint severity is lower than technology or distribution nodes.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest brand-level traffic, Olive Garden and LongHorn value perception, margin effect of menu engineering, commodity sensitivity, and evidence that scale purchasing is offsetting traffic softness.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Darden is a diversified casual-dining benchmark with strong evidence quality, purchasing scale, and clear brand-level traffic read-through. It ranks lower because its portfolio diversification lowers purity of any single value or traffic thesis and the market may already price its quality and scale advantages.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need updated traffic, ticket, loyalty active-member trends, mobile-order throughput, labor-hour investments, coffee/input inflation, China performance, and evidence that operational changes are improving wait times and frequency.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Starbucks is a global beverage, loyalty, digital-ordering, coffee-input, and store-throughput bellwether. It is highly falsifiable and evidence-rich, but the thesis depends on a turnaround in traffic, execution, and value perception rather than a hard supply-chain bottleneck.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest restaurant-equipment order trends, backlog, replacement versus new-unit demand, automation/beverage product adoption, customer concentration, tariff exposure, and proof that capex is being prioritized despite operator cost pressure.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Middleby maps to the kitchen-equipment and automation node: faster cooking, beverage systems, refrigeration, warming, and throughput improvements. It has a plausible labor-productivity chokepoint angle, but restaurant-specific public-market purity and direct demand evidence require more work.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need separation of traffic/order growth from price/mix, plus evidence that delivery aggregators, carryout value offers, and loyalty are strengthening franchisee economics rather than relying on promotion intensity.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: High-priority operator because Domino's directly tests several restaurant funnel nodes at once: delivery/carryout frequency, digital ordering, franchisee economics, value positioning, and food/labor cost pass-through. The business is highly mapped to the public market, and the key thesis can be tested through same-store sales, order counts, ticket, franchisee profitability, delivery economics, loyalty/digital mix, and unit growth.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need validation of competitive moat versus POS vendors, delivery platforms, payment processors, and in-house enterprise systems; also need proof that payments and guest-engagement modules can scale without margin dilution or customer churn.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong chokepoint-style software candidate because restaurant operators are prioritizing digital ordering, payments, loyalty, guest engagement, delivery-channel control, and data loops. Olo is a relatively pure public-market mapping to restaurant digital infrastructure rather than restaurant traffic alone. The opportunity is falsifiable through location count, average revenue per unit, module attach rates, payment adoption, net revenue retention, customer concentration, and competitive displacement.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that recent traffic and comp strength are durable after promotional laps, including guest frequency, margin impact, labor execution, commodity sensitivity, and Maggiano's drag or contribution.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Brinker is a high-beta casual-dining value-comeback test case. Chili's can validate whether advertising, menu simplification, everyday value, and menu innovation can drive sustained traffic after major comp laps. It has high falsifiability and mispricing potential, but lower durability and supplier scarcity.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need brand-level evidence separating Burger King turnaround, Tim Hortons coffee traffic, Popeyes chicken growth, and Firehouse expansion; consolidated numbers may hide uneven franchisee economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: High-priority franchisor platform because it tests QSR value perception, global unit growth, franchisee health, coffee frequency, burger/beef pressure, chicken exposure, remodel capex, and international expansion. Its multi-brand structure gives a broader restaurant read-through than a single-concept operator. Thesis validation is relatively clear through comparable sales, traffic, franchisee profitability, development pipeline, remodel pace, royalty growth, and margin bridge.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest evidence that same-store growth is transaction-led rather than price-led, and that franchisee returns remain attractive if chicken-wing costs normalize upward or promotional intensity rises.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Priority growth-franchise candidate because it cleanly exposes digital ordering, franchised unit growth, chicken-wing commodity sensitivity, and restaurant throughput. Its asset-light model gives a focused test of whether strong consumer frequency and franchisee returns can overcome input volatility. The thesis can be falsified through same-store sales quality, transaction growth, wing-cost changes, unit openings, franchisee cash-on-cash returns, and digital mix.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need clearer separation between true foodservice volume growth, pricing pass-through, new contract wins, and margin improvement from labor/procurement technology rather than mix or accounting effects.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Inference: Aramark is not a restaurant pure play, but it is a strong adjacent read-through for away-from-home food demand, labor planning, procurement scale, food inflation pass-through, and technology-enabled productivity. Fact: Q2 fiscal 2026 results showed strong organic revenue growth, productivity gains, supply-chain efficiencies, and management commentary around AI/menu and labor-planning tools. Serenity relevance is high because it tests whether scale procurement plus labor technology is a more durable chokepoint than individual restaurant concepts.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need store-level proof that Infinite Kitchen units sustain higher throughput, lower labor hours, better margins, and acceptable customer experience across multiple geographies rather than isolated pilot economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Hypothesis: Sweetgreen is the cleanest public-market test in this chunk for whether fast-casual restaurants can offset wage, produce, fuel, and traffic pressure through loyalty, menu innovation, and kitchen automation. Its Infinite Kitchen rollout, negative same-store-sales guidance, restaurant-level-margin guidance, and new-unit cadence create a highly measurable Serenity setup: if automation improves labor productivity and throughput while traffic stabilizes, the thesis strengthens; if same-store sales and margins remain weak, it fails quickly. Fact: the correct public ticker is SG, not SGV.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof that door rationalization and franchise mix shift can produce sustainable organic growth, not just near-term margin improvement from closing weak locations.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Hypothesis: Krispy Kreme is a high-falsifiability turnaround around delivered-fresh distribution, higher-volume doors, international franchising, and post-McDonald's reset. Fact: Q1 2026 results showed a strategic closure of underperforming doors, including former McDonald's USA partnership locations, and management emphasized U.S. profitability improvement and capital-light international franchising. The setup has mispricing potential because the failed McDonald's expansion damaged the growth narrative, while the revised model may be easier to evaluate through average weekly sales per door, adjusted EBITDA, and points-of-access quality.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof that new markets can sustain mature-store sales and margins without excessive labor, real-estate, or opening-cost pressure.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful growth-format candidate because beverage frequency, drive-thru throughput, labor scheduling, real-estate expansion, and coffee/input inflation are direct restaurant-funnel questions. Demand durability may be stronger than meal-based concepts if habitual beverage visits persist, but the bottleneck is less supply-scarce than software or distribution. The thesis is testable through new-unit productivity, same-shop transactions, ticket, labor hours, throughput, app/loyalty mix, and store-level margins.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that breakfast and value offers are expanding transactions profitably rather than pressuring franchisee margins amid beef and labor inflation.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Good QSR value-war candidate because Wendy's directly tests consumer price sensitivity, breakfast/daypart expansion, franchisee unit economics, beef-cost exposure, and promotional discipline. It is less differentiated as a chokepoint than USFD, Olo, or the higher-growth franchised platforms, but it has clean public-market purity and strong falsifiability through traffic, same-store sales, franchisee profitability, unit openings/closures, and commodity-cost commentary.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest traffic versus pricing mix, restaurant-level margin bridge, labor-productivity evidence, and proof that premium positioning remains resilient if consumers trade down.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong fast-casual test case for premium burger demand, restaurant-level margin recovery, throughput, urban/suburban traffic mix, kiosk/digital adoption, and beef-cost pressure. The public-market mapping is clean and the evidence path is straightforward. It ranks below the most compelling chokepoint candidates because it is more brand/operator-specific and less supply-scarce.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need franchisee-level evidence: unit margins, closures/openings, marketing ROI, delivery aggregator costs, and whether value promotions improve traffic without lowering franchisee cash flow.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Hypothesis: Papa John's is a pure but currently challenged test of pizza QSR value, delivery/carryout traffic, franchisee economics, and refranchising. Fact: Q1 2026 materials pointed to North America comparable-sales pressure, refranchising, and guidance for North America comparable sales down 2% to 4%, while international comparable sales were guided positive. Serenity relevance is in the turnaround falsification: value offers, loyalty, delivery economics, and franchisee health must stabilize North America without excessive discounting.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need customer/channel mix detail showing how much profit exposure is tied to QSR and restaurant foodservice versus retail, export, and commodity cycles.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Inference: Pilgrim's Pride is a relevant restaurant supply-chain node because chicken remains a key value protein for QSR sandwiches, wings, tenders, and menu substitution when beef is expensive. Fact: Q1 2026 commentary cited positive chicken fundamentals, affordability, foodservice momentum, and demand from key customers. Its bottleneck relevance is stronger than its restaurant-theme purity because it is a protein commodity and prepared-foods supplier rather than a restaurant operator.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need restaurant-channel revenue and margin disclosure by segment, including contract structures and whether restaurant customers absorb or resist beef and chicken price changes.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Inference: Tyson is a large protein-cost and menu-mix read-through for restaurants, especially beef, chicken, and prepared foods. Fact: Q2 fiscal 2026 results showed strong Chicken and Prepared Foods margins but a large Beef adjusted operating loss, matching the broader USDA evidence that cattle/beef supply remains constrained. Serenity relevance is highest as an input-cost/chokepoint monitor for restaurant concepts, not as a pure restaurant equity candidate.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need country-level same-store sales, traffic, royalty/rent burden, capex requirements, FX sensitivity, and evidence that consumer demand is not simply inflation-driven nominal growth.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful international franchisee/operator candidate because it separates franchisor economics from operator-level exposure to traffic, capex, FX, local inflation, labor, and emerging-market consumer demand. It may have higher mispricing potential because many U.S.-centric restaurant screens underweight Latin America operator dynamics, but the thesis depends heavily on country-level macro and currency variables.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need latest evidence on traffic versus check growth, labor productivity, menu simplification, food-cost bridge, and whether margin recovery is sustainable without cutting service quality.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Good full-service/casual-dining margin candidate because it is exposed to labor intensity, menu complexity, traffic, discretionary dining behavior, and commodity sensitivity. It helps test whether casual dining can defend traffic and margin without excessive discounting. It ranks lower because supplier scarcity is limited and the thesis is more execution-sensitive than chokepoint-driven.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need franchisee-level profitability, store closure/opening trends, remodel/reinvestment requirements, and evidence that traffic recovery is not purely promotion-driven.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Relevant franchised casual-dining platform because IHOP and Applebee's test value menus, franchisee health, brand reinvestment, and lower-to-middle-income consumer pressure. Mispricing potential may be higher if market narratives over- or understate brand deterioration, but the bottleneck quality is modest. Falsification is clear through franchisee closures, traffic, promotional mix, royalty health, and development pipeline.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence on traffic quality, beef-cost mitigation, discount intensity, store-level margin recovery, and whether turnaround actions improve unit economics rather than only reducing costs temporarily.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Relevant but higher-risk casual-dining and steakhouse candidate because it directly tests beef inflation, traffic, discounting, restaurant-level margins, and turnaround execution. It has clear falsifiability and potential mispricing if beef-cost or turnaround expectations are too pessimistic or optimistic, but it is not a scarce supply-chain node.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need restaurant-only delivery growth, Eats take rate, merchant economics, subscription engagement, ad revenue mix, regulatory labor-cost exposure, and clear separation from mobility and grocery performance.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Uber has meaningful restaurant-delivery exposure through Uber Eats and benefits from logistics density, but the restaurant-specific signal is diluted by mobility, grocery, advertising, and other delivery categories. It is useful as a comparative delivery-marketplace read-through but less pure than DoorDash.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof of franchisee profitability, net unit growth stabilization, traffic recovery, and sustainable value positioning without margin-destructive discounting.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Useful smaller QSR turnaround candidate because it tests value positioning, franchisee health, late-night/daypart traffic, unit closures/openings, and brand reinvestment. It may have mispricing potential because smaller restaurant platforms can re-rate sharply if unit economics stabilize, but the evidence burden is high and the competitive moat is less clear.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need more granular evidence on foodservice customer concentration, pricing power, volume versus price growth, and direct exposure to restaurants versus institutional foodservice.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Inference: Hormel is a prepared-foods and foodservice supplier with restaurant relevance through bacon, pepperoni, proteins, and value-added prepared items, but the theme purity is lower than operators and focused chicken suppliers. Fact: recent fiscal 2026 materials indicated the Foodservice segment remained a growth contributor and management expected mid-single-digit Foodservice growth. The Serenity angle is procurement and prepared-input resilience rather than a scarce chokepoint.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need segment-level detail separating restaurant-like foodservice from facilities management, education contract losses, healthcare cross-selling, currency effects, and pricing pass-through.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Inference: Sodexo is useful as a global contract-foodservice benchmark for labor, pricing, procurement, and institutional away-from-home demand, but it is less relevant to the U.S. restaurant theme than Aramark in this chunk. Fact: H1 fiscal 2026 results showed weak North America organic growth, Food services organic growth of only about 0.8%, margin pressure, and reduced guidance. This makes it a good negative-control candidate rather than a top chokepoint candidate.

ranked_candidates.company: The Manitowoc Company / Welbilt exposure note
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current public-market mapping for commercial foodservice equipment exposure, including which listed companies own relevant Welbilt assets or competing equipment lines, and whether restaurant capex is materially flowing into automation/throughput equipment.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Conceptually relevant because commercial kitchen equipment, refrigeration, beverage systems, and automation are plausible restaurant productivity chokepoints. However, this candidate has a ticker/company mapping problem and should not be treated as a validated public-market candidate until the listed exposure is cleaned up. It remains a coverage-gap placeholder rather than a ranked investable research lead.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need to remap the candidate from BERY to Amcor and then quantify restaurant/foodservice packaging exposure inside the combined company.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Fact: Berry Global is no longer a standalone public-market ticker after Amcor completed the Berry acquisition in 2025. As a restaurant packaging node, the business has relevance to off-premises demand, rigid/flexible packaging, and input costs, but the correct current public-market mapping is through Amcor rather than BERY. Serenity priority is therefore low for this specific candidate record, though the packaging node itself remains worth tracking.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need a replacement public-market mapping for the foodservice-packaging node, such as Amcor or other listed packaging suppliers, and evidence of restaurant-specific revenue exposure.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Fact: Pactiv Evergreen was acquired by Novolex and delisted in 2025, so it is not currently a standalone public-market candidate. The operating node, foodservice packaging, remains thematically relevant to takeout, delivery, packaging regulation, paper/plastic input costs, and restaurant cost control, but the ticker-level research priority is minimal because the public equity mapping is gone.

summary: Split Layer 3 ranking merged from candidate chunks.
